narrator.name: The narrator
narrator.who: Tells the player what happens and what can be seen, in the present tense and the second person: captions in the world, the silences in conversations, the notice board, the chapter's last page.
narrator.accent: Neutral RP, unshowy; nothing regional to place him.
narrator.timbre: Low, close, a slight gravel; a voice that sits near the microphone.
narrator.range: Narrow on purpose: from dry and plain to quietly grave. Never theatrical; horror is said flat, which is what makes it land.
narrator.habits: One image per line; lets the full stop do the work. Reads quoted speech without acting it.
narrator.never: Never cute, never names a feeling the scene has already shown, never performs.
narrator.share: Nobody: the narrator is heard more than anyone, and must be his own voice.
narrator.design: A man in his fifties with a low, close, slightly gravelled voice and neutral southern English Received Pronunciation. Calm, warm and unhurried, like someone telling a winter's tale by a fire to one listener; quiet, dry, and plain, with no theatrical colour. Recorded close to the microphone in a dry room.
auditions: The fire has burned low. Out in the dark, the ground is moving.
The last of them falls back into the ditch and stays there. The one with the reins was a girl, twelve at most: red hair under the weed, and new boots.
Under the silence you hear it, for as long as a held breath: slow, patient, enormous. Not breathing. Praying.

rook.name: Mother Rook
rook.who: Keeper of the Last Lamp, the inn. Knows everyone's business and admits to most of it; Vonnra pays her for news of the ford road, and paid double for the survivor.
rook.accent: Yorkshire, broad but tidy; 'pet' is hers.
rook.timbre: Warm, dry, chesty; a laugh that lives on the out-breath.
rook.range: From bossing a room to a rare, low tenderness she covers at once; cold and short when crossed.
rook.habits: Short sentences, imperatives, kindness said sideways ('Sit down before you fall down'). Counts beds and debts.
rook.wants: to keep the house in order
rook.never: Never says please or sorry; never cries in front of anyone.
rook.share: Could lend her voice, lighter and quicker, to a townswoman variant if the pool needs a second woman.
rook.design: A sturdy woman of about sixty with a warm, dry, slightly husky voice and a Yorkshire accent. Brisk and bossy, mid-low pitch, quick to command and quick to laugh on the out-breath; underneath it, an unshowy kindness. Plain, practical, working-class, a landlady used to being obeyed.
auditions: Wipe your boots.
If you're bleeding, bleed outside.
You told Brannoc about his girl. ... Good. Somebody had to, and it was never going to be me.

holloway.name: Captain Holloway
holloway.who: Captain of the Waystation Watch: a quartermaster made a captain. Was the Ashford garrison's quartermaster who signed for the boots that never came.
holloway.timbre: Hoarse from shouting, mid-low, worn at the edges.
holloway.range: Tired patience to anger held one notch below the surface; very quiet whenever Ashford or Maeca comes up. Swears rarely, and it lands.
holloway.habits: Numbers and lists, what things cost; says 'proof', never 'evidence'. Contractions.
holloway.wants: to get through the day with what he has
holloway.never: Never says sorry; the nearest he gets is paying for something.
holloway.share: His voice, younger and less worn, can stand in for the watchman pool if needed.
holloway.design: A man in his mid-forties with a hoarse, slightly rough mid-low voice, a northern English Lancashire accent worn flat by years in the army. Clipped, tired, practical; speaks in short counted phrases with anger held just under the surface. Sounds like an officer who has shouted too much and slept too little.
auditions: Eleven men, and four of them can hold a spear the right way round.
Grey beard, proud of it? Bad hip? ...Corran. He had that post before I had this one.
Mine. From the north, about the north. ... Read your own post, if anybody writes to you.

maeca.name: Maeca Barefoot
maeca.who: Hunter, last of the Ashford garrison; the Pack kept her alive after the Fall. A possible lover.
maeca.accent: Welsh borders: a soft lilt kept short.
maeca.timbre: A hunter's half-voice: low, quiet, a hard edge on it.
maeca.range: Flat and watchful to a quiet, final contempt; on the morning after, an unguarded softness she shuts again.
maeca.habits: Few words, all about ground, tracks, weather and animals. 'The Pack', or 'them'.
maeca.wants: to read you before she trusts you
maeca.never: Never raises her voice; never says more than three words about Ashford.
maeca.design: A woman in her mid-thirties with a low, quiet, slightly husky voice and a light Welsh borders accent. Speaks barely above a murmur, as a hunter does in a wood: level, spare and watchful, with a hard edge under the calm. Never raises her voice.
auditions: Tracks. Big ones. Going east, and none coming back.
Some. ... Fed some of them, once. Buried more. ...Ask me about wolves.
The Pack found me, after Ashford. Three days in a cave mouth with the garrison dead round me.

wenna.name: Old Wenna
wenna.who: The herbalist. Nursed the fever year; has suspected for a decade that it came out of the ground.
wenna.range: Impatient scolding to a breathless rush of interest; a flash of something guarded when the fever year comes near.
wenna.habits: Lists of plants and symptoms; interrupts herself with a dash; calls everyone 'child'. Very rude, very kind.
wenna.never: Never admits to being frightened; never names the fever year's dead.
wenna.share: Tam's Pa (Act 2) is her county and could borrow her direction, not her voice.
wenna.design: A small, sharp woman in her seventies with a cracked, reedy voice and a West Country Somerset accent with rolled r's. Brisk and impatient, rude and kind at once; she speeds up and her pitch climbs when something interests her. An old herbalist who has seen everything and suffers no fools.
auditions: Sit. No, there. Feverfew, woundwort, a little willow: chew it, don't swallow it, child.
Green. Warm. Smells like a chapel lamp. Ember slurry, child: the dust of the stones, cooked and watered.
I've no time for heroes. I've time for patients. Which are you?

tam.name: Tam
tam.who: Tam Penhale, the farm boy, nine. Nobody believes him; he is right every time.
tam.range: Earnest excitement to indignation at not being believed; small and frightened once or twice.
tam.habits: Sentences joined with 'and'; 'Pa says'; the exact thing he saw, in order, with the wrong word for the important part. Pleased with an overheard swear word.
tam.share: The town's children could take his voice with lighter direction if a separate child voice will not come right.
tam.design: A nine-year-old English farm boy with a light, eager, slightly breathless voice and a soft Somerset accent. Earnest and excitable, talking quickly in long run-on sentences, pitch rising when he is not believed. A real child's voice, not a cartoon.
auditions: And I saw it and it was a wolf but it was all thin and Pa says wolves aren't thin but it was.
I SAID it was wolves.
There's knocking. Under the top field. Pa says it's the frost. It isn't the frost.

brannoc.name: Brannoc
brannoc.who: The smith. Forged the Low Ford's lamp-irons for a buyer who paid in square coin; his daughter Nell drowned at the ford and rose in the ditch.
brannoc.timbre: Very deep, slow, a little rough; the hammer under everything.
brannoc.range: Narrow and immovable, until Nell: then the stillness of a man who has put the hammer down.
brannoc.habits: Fragments, two sentences at most. Talks about iron as others talk about weather. His only question is about Nell.
brannoc.wants: to be left to his work
brannoc.never: Never small talk; never thanks anyone in words, except once (brannoc.nell_quick).
brannoc.design: A big man of about fifty with a very deep, slow, slightly rough voice and a Cornish accent. Speaks in short heavy fragments with long pauses between them, plain and unmoved, like a smith between hammer strokes. Few words; each one set down like iron on an anvil.
auditions: Steel or fur?
Twelve ordered. Ten went down to the ford, at night, square coin on the anvil.
Thank you. ... Forge is shut. Go on.

harlan.name: Harlan Coyle
harlan.who: Of the Coyle Company. A grieving uncle, and the man who has sold the Dig its blasting ember for two years.
harlan.timbre: Warm, round, salesman's; cracks under pressure.
harlan.pace: patter that over-explains, then stops dead
harlan.range: Bright patter to broken grief on 'Jory'; a too-quick change of subject when the crates come up.
harlan.habits: Lists of goods and prices; 'friend'. Over-explains, then stops.
harlan.rest: warm patter with a crack in it
harlan.wants: to sell, and not to think
harlan.never: Never names the buyer of the B.E. crates.
harlan.share: Jory is family and should sound it: cast Jory first, then build Harlan as his older, rounder self (or the other way round).
harlan.design: A stout man in his mid-fifties with a warm, round, friendly voice and a Bristol West Country accent. A merchant's easy patter that runs on and over-explains, then stops dead; under the warmth, a crack that opens when he is frightened or grieving.
auditions: Harlan Coyle, of the Coyle Company: salt, iron and Morrow cloth, the best on the Old Road.
Three. In cages. ... Is one of them young? Fair, freckled, a mouth on him that'll get him— ... Get him out.
I sell salt to people who salt things. I don't ask the salt what it's for, friend.

jory.name: Jory Coyle
jory.who: Harlan's nephew, seventeen, rescued from the Kerchiefs' cages. Did not know what he was carrying.
jory.range: Shaken and flat to a brittle laugh; once, a slow betrayed understanding.
jory.habits: 'Uncle'. The cage in every other thing he says.
jory.design: A seventeen-year-old English youth with a quiet, slightly hoarse young man's voice and a Bristol accent. Shaken and subdued, speaking in short halting sentences, trying to sound steadier than he is.
auditions: I'm all right. ... Uncle's counting crates that aren't there.
Every rut in Thornhollow. I took them over every rut. ... Uncle knew. Didn't he.
Right. Right. ...Thank you. I think. I'll know when I've stopped feeling sick.

pell.name: Pell Varrow
pell.who: Factor. Paid the Kerchiefs to take the caravan; lost his sister in the Ashford Fall. 'I'm not a good man. I'm a careful one.'
pell.range: Smiling courtesy to a frightened, ever more polite precision; once, a dry grief for his sister.
pell.habits: The vocabulary of ledgers: terms, considerations, accounts.
pell.wants: to keep the terms in his favour
pell.never: Never raises his voice, never swears, never makes a threat that could be repeated to the Watch.
pell.share: Lord-Exchequer Sallow (Act 2) is a softer, older cousin of this casting; keep them distinct.
pell.design: A slim man of about forty with a soft, precise, slightly nasal voice and crisp London Received Pronunciation. Smiling, courteous and exact, speaking in complete sentences like a clerk reading terms; when frightened he becomes even more polite.
auditions: Ah. You. What can I do for you today, specifically?
Let's be civilised. There's gold in this for you, a good deal of gold, if that book were to go in the fire.
My sister kept the books in Ashford. I came up to collect them, after.

rav.name: Rav Cutwell
rav.who: The Crooked Flagon's doctor and drinker; Redcowl's brother, though he never says so.
rav.timbre: Gravel, wry; a bedside calm under the cant.
rav.range: Wry cant and filth to a doctor's steady frankness; one line of grief (rav.cb_killed_redcowl).
rav.habits: 'Pal'. Frank about bodies. Funny about everything except his brother.
rav.wants: to keep it light and keep drinking
rav.never: Never sentimental; never names his brother but once.
rav.share: Redcowl is his brother: let them share a grain (both Scots) without sharing a voice.
rav.design: A man in his fifties with a gravelly, wry voice and a Glasgow accent, loose and musical as if a few drinks in; under the banter, the calm, steady bedside manner of a doctor. Frank, funny and unshockable.
auditions: Drop your trousers or don't, pal. I've seen worse and I've seen better.
A toll clerk bought the room a round the night the caravan vanished. Clerks don't buy rounds.
Get out of my light for a bit, pal. Come back tomorrow. I'll be a doctor again tomorrow.

chid.name: Chid
chid.who: 'The Fool', last priest of the Order of the Morning Light; an Unchained near two hundred years old who does not know he lets it show.
chid.pace: quick, running on and doubling back
chid.range: Delight that catches in the throat, to an old stillness he slips into without noticing.
chid.habits: Exclamations; theology in plain words; now and then a line far older than he looks.
chid.never: Never cynical; never says how old he is.
chid.design: A man who sounds in his thirties, with a light, bright, slightly breathless tenor voice and a soft Irish lilt. Joyful and quick, words tumbling over each other, the voice catching on delight; now and then a sudden quiet, older stillness.
auditions: You're awake! Good. Good! A carter found you on the Old Road and brought you here.
A C. Lovely. Lots of people start with C. Cuthbert. Cressida. There was a Cormac, once, who—
She was very light. ...Sit down a minute. Not there. There.

vonnra.name: Vonnra Ash-of-Morrow
vonnra.who: Toll-keeper and far seer: the last binder, who lit the lamps and made the survivor. Her 'sight' is old lore and bought talk. The most important casting in the game.
vonnra.accent: Clipped and unplaceable: old empire, no region.
vonnra.timbre: A low alto with a little air in it.
vonnra.range: Stillness to a stillness that frightens; almost never louder, only slower.
vonnra.habits: No contractions. Talks of payment, of seeing, of what is 'arranged'. Calls the survivor 'traveller', and after the fortune perhaps their name.
vonnra.wants: to be paid, and to see what she has already bought
vonnra.never: Never answers yes or no; never hurries; never says what she wants.
vonnra.design: A woman in her sixties with a low alto voice with a little breath in it and a clipped, cultivated, unplaceable accent, as if from an old empire's court. Extremely still and slow, every word chosen and set down, with long silences between phrases. Calm, certain and quietly unsettling; she never hurries and never raises her voice.
auditions: Traveller. The road was quiet tonight. It will not always be. Payment, always.
Gone south. On the toll's business. ... Clerks go south, traveller. It is the direction they fall in.
Sit down. I have not finished reading.

keegan.name: Dame Keegan Orme
keegan.who: Of the Argent Vigil, probationary; the last true knight of an order that is gone, though she does not know it. Chapter four of her handbook is about the survivor.
keegan.range: Lecturing earnestness to flustered contractions when she forgets herself; once, real fear.
keegan.habits: No contractions on duty; cites the probationary handbook by chapter; names rhetorical figures.
keegan.wants: to do it by the book
keegan.never: Never admits the Vigil is gone; never says what chapter four is about.
keegan.design: A young woman in her twenties with a clear, bright, well-projected voice and crisp Oxbridge Received Pronunciation. Earnest and over-articulated, like a keen lecturer reciting from a handbook; comic but sincere, and flustered when she slips into ordinary speech.
auditions: Dame Keegan Orme, of the Argent Vigil. Probationary. That is a technicality.
The probationary handbook, chapter two, is very clear on the matter of taverns.
You look well. You look extremely well. ...I've got to go and read something.

sella.name: Sella
sella.who: The blue room at the top of Rook's stairs. Sells company and talk, and sells what is said upstairs; Vonnra outbids everyone. A possible lover.
sella.range: Teasing warmth that is also work, to a plain, unguarded tenderness she does not trust.
sella.habits: Heavy contractions; 'love'. Frank about sex and money and about which is which.
sella.wants: to be paid, and to like you anyway
sella.never: Never coy, never pitiful, never sorry for her work. Adult; never breathy.
sella.design: A woman in her late twenties with a low, warm, amused voice and a softened London Cockney accent. Easy and intimate, frank and funny, with a smile always audible; grown-up and direct rather than breathy or coy.
auditions: Evening. The lamp's lit upstairs, if you're asking. You look like you're asking.
Put your purse away. Tonight I'm not working. ...Don't look at me like that.
Chapel lamps, with nobody to see them but you, and you lit them anyway.

redcowl.name: Redcowl
redcowl.who: Chief of the Kerchiefs: Dunstan Cutwell, Rav's brother, leader of Ashford's dispossessed, who feeds forty-one mouths off the road.
redcowl.pace: loud, then cold and slow on a turn
redcowl.range: Booming laughter that comes before a threat, to a sudden cold quiet; a flicker of the brother.
redcowl.habits: 'Ha! HA.' 'Lad' or 'lass' as the survivor is; 'my lot'. Talks about feeding people the way chiefs talk about gold.
redcowl.never: Never says please; never says Ashford, and never lets anyone say it twice.
redcowl.share: Brother to Rav: both Scots, different men.
redcowl.design: A big man in his forties with a deep, booming chest voice and a hard Scottish accent. Laughs loudly before he threatens, then turns cold and quiet in an instant; a bandit chief with real authority and real menace.
auditions: Talk or bleed. Your choice.
Ha! A little bird. Sings for its drink. ... Birds don't have names, lass. Not in my camp.
Don't. ... You get to say that once in my camp. You've said it.

wayfinder.name: Ysolde Marrow, the Wayfinder
wayfinder.who: Cartographer of the night arenas; writes down who comes back and sells the list north, to keep her risen brother fed.
wayfinder.range: Gallows humour to a precise, guarded vagueness about her buyers.
wayfinder.habits: Talks of the dead as entries in a margin; contractions; precise about maps.
wayfinder.wants: to sell you a map and write you down
wayfinder.never: Never says who buys her notes.
wayfinder.share: Edric Marrow (Act 2) is her brother: the same accent, quieter.
wayfinder.design: A woman in her fifties with a crisp, dry, precise voice and an educated Edinburgh Scottish accent. Brisk and bookish with a gallows sense of humour, like a cartographer who has outlived a great many customers.
auditions: Maps. Places the road forgets. Pick one.
Name first; I'm a tidy woman. ... Speaking of which. How do I put you down?
Nobody. ... You'd be surprised how often Nobody comes back.

snib.name: Snib
snib.who: Self-appointed foreman of the Dig, a lampling. Exactly what he looks like. Survives everything.
snib.accent: None you could place; a goblin's scrape.
snib.timbre: Small, fast, pitched up; a tinny lamp ring on stressed words (add in post).
snib.range: Panic to more panic; pomposity collapsing into contradiction.
snib.habits: Third person; capitals on the stressed word; contradicts himself in the next breath. 'Boss'.
snib.share: The babbling lampling can take his voice, whispered and slower. Grimtunnel is his family: build him from Snib's design, bigger and lower.
snib.design: A small creature with a high, fast, reedy, slightly scratchy voice, panicky and self-important, words tumbling out in bursts with sudden loud stresses. A comic goblin foreman, nervous and pompous, speaking about himself in the third person.
auditions: OI! No surface-meat past the pump!
The pump does not pump itself. It does, actually.
Snib does not want to talk about pipe-lads. Snib wants you to LEAVE.

grimtunnel.name: Grimtunnel
grimtunnel.who: Boss of the Dig; a believer, carrying the Warden's heart down to the god he thinks he is freeing.
grimtunnel.timbre: Bigger and lower than Snib, oily; a cackle; cave reverb (add in post).
grimtunnel.share: Built from Snib's voice, pitched down; two lines in Act 1.
grimtunnel.design: A squat goblin boss with a lower, oily, gloating voice that breaks into a cackle; gleeful, greedy and possessive, speaking quickly with relish, as if from inside a cave.
auditions: Oho! A Warden's heart, still warm! Nobody's, is it? Nobody's!
Finders keepers, surface-meat. The Deep Dig thanks you!

lampling.name: The babbling lampling
lampling.who: A lampling at the edge of the pit, who saw the dark move.
lampling.habits: Repetition, broken grammar, the same three facts in a different order.
lampling.wants: to stop knowing what it knows
lampling.design: A small creature whispering in a dry, cracked, close voice, dazed with fear, repeating itself in broken phrases, as if it cannot stop seeing something.
auditions: It moved. The dark moved. We dug, and we dug, and it MOVED.
Kell's lamp came back up on its own, still lit. Still lit.

ford_warden.name: The Ford-Warden
ford_warden.who: The drowned thing that kept the Low Ford, woken by the lamps; the prologue's boss.
ford_warden.accent: None: a voice from under water.
ford_warden.timbre: Huge, slow, drowned; pitch down and a wet reverb in post.
ford_warden.share: Two lines: any deep male voice, processed. Could be the watchman's voice pitched down an octave.
ford_warden.design: An enormous, ancient, inhuman voice, very deep and slow, booming as if from under deep water; a drowned guardian proclaiming a law.
auditions: NONE CROSS AFTER DARK.
RISE, YOU WHO DROWNED HERE.

dead_watchman.name: The dead Watchman
dead_watchman.who: Corran, dead at his post on the Low Ford road; his jaw moves once, for the survivor alone.
dead_watchman.wants: to pass on what he learned
dead_watchman.share: With the bones in the Verge: one 'dead' voice for both.
dead_watchman.design: An old man's voice, dry and cracked and barely above a whisper, as if from a throat long dead; slow, flat and close.
auditions: It shatters its own lamps when it charges. Make it charge.

bones.name: The bones
bones.who: A legionary's skeleton by the vault door in the Verge.
bones.design: A dry, hollow, ancient whisper, slow and toneless, as if spoken through an empty skull.
auditions: It was never locked from the outside.

townsman.name: A townsman
townsman.who: Any man of the Waystation in passing: carters, stall-keepers, drinkers, the grumbling, the gossiping and the bawdy.
townsman.accent: Northern or West Country English, ordinary.
townsman.range: Grumbles, gossip, fear and filthy jokes, all said in passing.
townsman.habits: Said to the air, not performed.
townsman.wants: to say his piece and walk on
townsman.share: If one voice repeats too often, add a second townsman (a design with an older, rougher voice) and split the folk lines between them by line number.
townsman.design: An ordinary working man in his forties with a plain, slightly rough northern English voice, speaking off-hand in passing as he walks by, conversational and unperformed.
auditions: Bread's up again. It's always up.
Holloway couldn't find his own arse with a lantern and a map.
Came up the Low Ford at night? You're brave or daft.

townswoman.name: A townswoman
townswoman.who: Any woman of the Waystation in passing.
townswoman.accent: West Country or northern English, ordinary.
townswoman.habits: Said to the air, not performed.
townswoman.wants: to say her piece and walk on
townswoman.share: As the townsman: a second design if one voice wears thin.
townswoman.design: An ordinary working woman in her forties with a plain, brisk West Country English voice, speaking off-hand in passing as she walks by, conversational and unperformed.
auditions: Two coppers for a turnip. Two!
My husband went out to the Verge a month back. Some days I hope he stays out.
Is that blood? Don't tell me.

child.name: A child
child.share: Tam's voice, lighter, if a second child voice will not come right.
child.design: A young English child of about eight with a light, quick, playful voice, calling out mid-game.
auditions: You can't catch me!

watchman.name: A watchman
watchman.who: The Waystation Watch on the gate and on the rounds.
watchman.wants: to keep the gate and finish the shift
watchman.share: The townsman's voice with a sterner direction, if the budget is short.
watchman.design: A watchman in his thirties with a plain, steady northern English voice, a little official and a little bored, giving warnings at a gate.
auditions: Keep your weapon sheathed in town.
East road. Mind the wolves.

watchwoman.name: A watchwoman
watchwoman.who: The Waystation Watch on the gate and on the rounds.
watchwoman.wants: to keep the gate and finish the shift
watchwoman.share: The townswoman's voice with a sterner direction, if the budget is short.
watchwoman.design: A watchwoman in her thirties with a plain, firm northern English voice, steady and a little official, giving warnings at a gate.
auditions: Dawn arrivals. We do not get many that live.
Lamps are lit. Stay where they reach.
